title: A New Theory of Disuse https://bjorklab.psych.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/13/2016/07/RBjork_EBjork_1992.pdf
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), November 19, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Craig Barton summarises Robert A. Bjork and Elizabeth Ligon Bjork's theoretical paper on why we forget, which proposes that forgetting is driven by interference from other learned material rather than simple decay. The Bjorks introduce their new theory of disuse as an alternative to Estes' older stimulus fluctuation model, arguing that disuse offers a fuller account of memory phenomena. Central to the theory is the idea that a memory trace's accessibility fades if it goes unused, even though the underlying storage strength of a well-learned memory persists. Repeated exposure and use of information increases how durably it is encoded, making it more resistant to this loss of accessibility. Barton notes the paper is purely theoretical, presenting no new experimental data, but draws out classroom-relevant principles about why periodic review keeps knowledge retrievable. The piece functions as an early conceptual foundation for later, more practical desirable-difficulties research from the same authors.
points: Forgetting is framed as a retrieval problem (disuse/interference), not permanent deletion — memory traces can lose accessibility while remaining intact in storage.
The Bjorks' disuse theory is positioned as a more complete rival to Estes' stimulus fluctuation model for explaining forgetting.
Repeated, spaced exposure to material increases how durably it gets encoded, directly supporting the case for periodic review over one-off teaching.
Because the paper is theoretical rather than experimental, Barton flags that its classroom implications must be inferred rather than taken as directly tested findings.
quotes: Repeated exposure to a stimulus over time increases its accessibility in memory.
The accessibility of a memory trace decays over time if it is not used.
The concept of disuse suggests that it is important to continue to use information that has been learned in order to maintain its accessibility.
The theory of disuse posits that memory traces weaken over time due to a lack of use.
The theory of stimulus fluctuation suggests that memory traces fluctuate in accessibility due to random variations in neural activity.
We feel that our theory of disuse provides a more complete explanation for forgetting than the theory of stimulus fluctuation.
